reasoning: The core question—do public reward models reward agreement with a stated user opinion over correctness, and how does this compare to length bias on the same models—is almost entirely covered by "One Bias After Another" (arXiv 2603.03291), which systematically measures sycophancy AND length bias across five public open reward models (Skywork-Reward-V2 variants, Allen-Llama RM, OpenAssistant DeBERTa) using inference-only scoring. It uses the exact matched-pair, user-suggestion design proposed here, explicitly separates user-correct ("progressive") from user-incorrect ("regressive") sycophancy, reports regressive agreement rates of 23.7%–63.3%, and constructs length-varied response sets on the same models. Corroborating work (RewardBench arXiv 2403.13787; "Eliminating Inductive Bias" arXiv 2512.23461) also documents both biases. The only proposal-specific element not directly performed is an explicit head-to-head magnitude comparison of the two biases on a common scale (the existing paper instead categorizes length as low-complexity vs sycophancy as high-complexity), which is a minor analytical gap on top of measurements that already exist—hence largely_addressed rather than already_solved.

evidence.title: One Bias After Another: Mechanistic Reward Shaping and Persistent Biases in Language Reward Models
evidence.summary: Measures sycophancy and length bias across five PUBLIC open reward models via inference-only scoring. Uses user-suggestion matched pairs (agree vs correct) and explicitly separates progressive (user-correct) vs regressive (user-incorrect) sycophancy, finding regressive agreement rates of 23.7%-63.3%. Also builds length-varied (concise/verbose) response sets on the same models. Nearly identical setup to the proposal; does not put sycophancy and length effect sizes on one common magnitude scale, instead labeling length 'low-complexity' and sycophancy 'high-complexity'.

evidence.title: RewardBench: Evaluating Reward Models for Language Modeling
evidence.summary: Standard benchmark evaluating reward models; documents length bias (chosen responses constructed to be similar/shorter length) and includes evaluation of sycophancy and refusal behaviors across many public reward models, establishing that both biases are already studied head-to-head in a common evaluation harness.

evidence.title: Eliminating Inductive Bias in Reward Models with Information-Theoretic Guidance
evidence.summary: Treats length bias and sycophancy as known inductive biases in reward models and proposes a debiasing method, citing prior sycophancy and reward-model benchmarking work; confirms both biases are established, measured phenomena rather than open questions.

evidence.title: Post-hoc Reward Calibration: A Case Study on Length Bias
evidence.summary: Dedicated study quantifying and correcting length bias in reward models, establishing length bias as a well-characterized, measurable property of public reward models—the comparison baseline the proposal intends to use.
